distr::NormalTrunc¶

The truncated normal distribution: a normal distribution restricted to an interval.

Signature¶

pluss::Series distr::pdf(dst::NormalTrunc, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::logpdf(dst::NormalTrunc, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::cdf(dst::NormalTrunc, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::logcdf(dst::NormalTrunc, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::sample(dst::NormalTrunc, const std::vector<double>& params, std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes, pluss::Config cfg = {}, std::uint64_t seed = 0);

What It Does¶

The truncated normal distribution is a normal distribution conditioned to lie between lower and upper: the density is the normal one inside the interval, rescaled to integrate to one, and zero outside. It models a measurement that can only be observed in a range (a test score between 0 and 100, a size above a cut-off), and it is the posterior of a normal quantity under a hard constraint. Its mean lies between the mean of the untruncated normal and the middle of the interval.

The kind-based functions take {lower, upper, mean, sd}; the object is distr::NormalTrunc{lower, upper, mean, stddev}.

The parameters, in the order of the params list:

Parameter

Constraint

Meaning

lower

lower < upper

the lower truncation point

upper

lower < upper

the upper truncation point

mean

any real

the mean of the untruncated normal

sd

> 0

the standard deviation of the untruncated normal

Support: the interval [lower, upper].

The object form of this family, with the same functions as methods, is on its own page: distr::NormalTrunc.

Parameters¶

const pluss::Series& x

The points at which to evaluate, a Series of any shape; the result has the same shape. Points outside the support have density zero and distribution value 0 or 1.

const std::vector<double>& params

The parameters of the family, in the order shown in the table above. A list of the wrong length is refused.

std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes

The shape of the array of random draws, for example {n} or {rows, columns}.

pluss::Config cfg

The dtype and platform of the draws; the default is Float32 on the CPU, so request Float64 when precision matters.

std::uint64_t seed

The seed of the stream. The same seed always gives the same draws; a seed of 0 is a fixed default, not a random one.

Returns¶

pdf, logpdf, cdf and logcdf return a Series of the shape of x; sample returns a Series of the requested shape.

Errors¶

  • Parameters outside their valid range are refused with an error that names the requirement (lower must be less than upper and sd positive).

  • A params list of the wrong length is refused.

Practical Examples¶

Example 1¶

Example 1 evaluates the density (mass) function, the distribution function and the log-density of the NormalTrunc on a small grid with distr::pdf, distr::cdf and distr::logpdf.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);

  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.5, -1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0}, f64);
  const std::vector<double> params = {-1.0, 2.0, 0.0, 1.0};

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "pdf:";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::NormalTrunc, x, params).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "cdf:";
  for (double v : distr::cdf(dst::NormalTrunc, x, params).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "logpdf:";
  for (double v : distr::logpdf(dst::NormalTrunc, x, params).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
}

Output

x: -1.50000 -1.00000 -0.50000 0.00000 1.00000 2.00000
pdf: 0.00000 0.29559 0.43009 0.48735 0.29559 0.06596
cdf: 0.00000 0.00000 0.18310 0.41699 0.83398 1.00000
logpdf: -inf -1.21877 -0.84377 -0.71877 -1.21877 -2.71877

The density is largest on this grid at x = 0, where it is 0.48735; the distribution function runs from 0 at x = -1.5 to 1 at x = 2, and it is the running total of the density. logpdf is the logarithm of the density, for example log(0.48735) = -0.71877 at x = 0; where the density is zero (outside the support) the logarithm is -inf.

Example 2¶

Example 2 checks that the three descriptions of the same probability agree: the integral of the density (sum of the masses) over a range, the difference of the distribution function at its ends, and the fraction of random draws that land in it.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);
  const std::vector<double> params = {-1.0, 2.0, 0.0, 1.0};

  // The three ways to the probability that the variable lies in [-0.5, 1.5]:
  const auto grid = pluss::series::linspace(-0.5, 1.5, 3001, f64);
  const double area = as_f64(distr::pdf(dst::NormalTrunc, grid, params).antidiff(grid).trapezoid());

  const auto edges = pluss::make_series({-0.5, 1.5}, f64);
  const auto c = distr::cdf(dst::NormalTrunc, edges, params).pull<double>();

  const auto draws = distr::sample(dst::NormalTrunc, params, {200000}, f64, 7ULL);
  const double fraction = as_f64(((draws >= -0.5).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64) * (draws <= 1.5).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64)).mean());

  std::cout << "integral of the density: " << area << '\n';
  std::cout << "cdf(1.5) - cdf(-0.5): " << c[1] - c[0] << '\n';
  std::cout << "fraction of 200000 draws in range: " << fraction << '\n';
}

Output

integral of the density: 0.76308
cdf(1.5) - cdf(-0.5): 0.76308
fraction of 200000 draws in range: 0.76248

The integral of the density (0.76308) and the difference of the distribution function (0.76308) agree to all printed digits: they are two computations of one probability. The fraction of random draws (0.76248) differs from it by 6.00e-04, which is the size of the sampling error of a fraction of 200000 draws (a standard error of about 9.51e-04), so the density, the distribution function and the sampler describe the same distribution.

Example 3¶

Example 3 shows how the shape changes with the parameters: the density at the same points for 3 parameter settings.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0}, f64);

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "mean -1:";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::NormalTrunc, x, {-1.0, 2.0, -1.0, 1.0}).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "mean 0 :";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::NormalTrunc, x, {-1.0, 2.0, 0.0, 1.0}).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "mean 3 :";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::NormalTrunc, x, {-1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 1.0}).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
}

Output

x: -1.0000 -0.5000 0.0000 0.5000 1.0000 1.5000 2.0000
mean -1: 0.8000 0.7060 0.4853 0.2597 0.1083 0.0352 0.0089
mean 0 : 0.2956 0.4301 0.4874 0.4301 0.2956 0.1582 0.0660
mean 3 : 0.0008 0.0055 0.0279 0.1105 0.3404 0.8165 1.5254

Read down the rows: mean -1 peaks on this grid at x = -1 (value 0.8); mean 0 peaks on this grid at x = 0 (value 0.4874); mean 3 peaks on this grid at x = 2 (value 1.5254). The parameters move the location, the width and the shape of the curve, which is what choosing a member of the family means.
